pages.title: Planning your day around the light
pages.description: How to plan a wedding day around golden hour, from Larchmere.
pages.intro: Why the hour before sunset matters, and how to find it for your date.

blocks.heading: What golden hour is
blocks.body:
When the sun is low, between a few degrees above the horizon and just below it, its light is warm and soft and comes from the side. That's the hour, give or take, before sunset. In June in southern England it starts after half past eight in the evening; in late September, around half past six; in December, before three.

Our light planner works it out for your date and place from the sun's position, to the nearest minute.

blocks.alt: A couple standing on stone by a lake in late sun
blocks.caption: Wrenmoor Hall. Demo photograph.

blocks.heading: Planning with it
blocks.body: In summer, golden hour falls after the meal; we ask for twenty to forty minutes of you then. In winter it can come before the ceremony ends, so we take portraits straight after the vows. Either way, tell your venue early: some will hold the speeches for you.

pages.title: Wedding timelines that work
pages.description: How to plan a wedding day timeline, from Larchmere.
pages.intro: What we've learnt from the days that ran to time, and the ones that didn't.

blocks.heading: Give everything a little more time
blocks.body: Getting ready always takes longer than planned. So do group photographs, unless you give us a list. The days that run to time have half an hour spare before the ceremony and ten minutes between everything else.

blocks.alt: A groom laughing under palm trees, string lights overhead
blocks.caption: Demo photograph.

blocks.heading: Put the speeches before the food goes cold
blocks.body: Or after it, but decide early, and tell the kitchen. Our day planner builds a first draft from your ceremony time; your venue will know the rest.

questions.q: How far ahead do couples book?
questions.a: Most book twelve to eighteen months ahead, summer Saturdays first. Check your date above; it takes a minute.

questions.q: How do we hold our date?
questions.a: A third of the price holds it, by the payment link we send with the contract.

questions.q: Will you be in the way?
questions.a: We work quietly, with small cameras and no lights during the ceremony. Most guests forget we're there.

questions.q: Do you record the vows and the speeches?
questions.a: Yes, with small microphones we fit before the ceremony and on the speakers' table.
Where the venue and the airspace allow it, and only in dry, calm weather, so we never promise it.

questions.q: Do we need to feed you?
questions.a: A hot meal for each of us when your guests eat, please. We'll eat out of sight and be back before the speeches.

questions.q: When do we get our film?
questions.a: Three photographs and a few seconds of film the next morning, then the rest as the timeline shows.
We choose licensed music that fits your day, and ask you first if you have a song in mind.
Only if you say yes. Your film is yours; we ask before showing any of it.
Anywhere. Travel within mainland Britain is in the price; abroad, we quote flights and a night's stay.

questions.q: Can we see how our film is coming along?
questions.a: Yes. We send you a code; your page shows where your film is (footage in, the edit, colour, sound, delivered) and when your trailer is due.

questions.q: Can you fly the drone at our venue?
questions.a: Only where the venue agrees and the airspace allows it. Our venues page lists the rule at each venue we know.

venues.drone: We fly a drone only where the venue agrees, in dry, calm weather, and never over guests. Since 1 January 2026, anyone flying a drone of 100g or more in the UK needs a Flyer ID, and a camera drone of 100g or more also needs an Operator ID. A drone must never be more than 120 metres above the ground. Near airports, no one may fly in the flight restriction zone without the airport's permission, so some venues can't be filmed from the air at all.

dayPlanner.title: Your day, around the light
dayPlanner.intro: How we film a wedding, hour by hour, and a plan for yours built from your ceremony time and that evening's golden hour.
dayPlanner.message: Hello Larchmere, here's the plan for our day.

explained.heading: Before the ceremony
explained.body:
We arrive two hours before, one of us with each of you. Details first: the dress, the rings, the letters. Then the people, while there's still time to talk.

We fit small microphones before the ceremony, so the vows sound like they did in the room.

photo.alt: A guest at an iron gate, laughing, waiting for the ceremony
photo.caption: Before the ceremony. Demo photograph.

explained.heading: The ceremony
explained.body: Two cameras, no lights, no moving about during the vows. If your registrar or minister has rules about where we stand, we follow them; most churches ask, and some don't allow filming at all, so we check first.

photo.alt: The groom lifting the veil, guests watching
photo.caption: The ceremony. Demo photograph.

explained.heading: Drinks, the meal, the speeches
explained.body: Group photographs are quick: ten minutes, a list you give us, someone who knows the families to call names. During the meal we eat too, out of sight. Speeches we film from two sides, with sound from the microphone and our own.

explained.heading: Golden hour
explained.body: The hour or so before sunset is when skin, dresses and trees look their best. We find it for your date and place, and ask for twenty to forty minutes of you, away from your guests. In winter it often falls before the ceremony ends; then we take portraits straight after it.

photo.alt: Hands held in low sun, a ring catching the light
photo.caption: Golden hour. Demo photograph.

explained.heading: The first dance, and goodbye
explained.body: We stay for the first dance and half an hour after, longer if golden hour comes late. Then we go home and back up every card twice before we sleep.

musicPage.title: Music and licensing
musicPage.intro: Why your film has the music it has, and what churches ask before a ceremony is filmed.

photo.alt: The vows in a white room, the minister reading
photo.caption: Demo photograph.

sections.heading: Why we use licensed music
sections.body:
A wedding film with a commercial song in it can't be shared online without permission from the people who own that music. For a cover version, that means a synchronisation licence too.

So every film we make uses music licensed for films like yours, from libraries that grant those rights. Your film can then go wherever you want to put it.

sections.heading: If you have a song in mind
sections.body: Tell us. We'll look for it, or for something with the same feel, in what we're licensed to use. Your first dance, played live or from a speaker at the venue, is part of your day, and we film it as it happened.

sections.heading: Filming in a church
sections.body:
The Church of England asks couples to talk to their vicar about filming in advance. Copyrighted music, poetry and readings shouldn't be recorded without the owners' permission: many churches hold a Church Copyright Licence that covers recording live music, and without one a Limited Manufacture Licence from PRS for Music is usually needed. Organists and choirs may ask an extra fee for being filmed, and some churches don't allow filming during the ceremony at all.

We ask your vicar for you, and tell you what they say.

sections.heading: Register offices and venues
sections.body: Registrars and venues set their own rules about where we stand and what we film. We ask before the day, and follow them.
